extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties litigating inter partes proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural standards for taking discovery depositions (oral or written) and for making documents of record in Board inter partes proceedings, including domestic and foreign depositions, subpoenas, letters rogatory, and related timing and notice requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making documents of record via requests for admission and notice of reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence or documents obtained through discovery (e.g., responses or disclosures) may be used by serving an opponent a request for admission of the genuineness of the subject documents, which should be attached as exhibits to the request for admission; then, during its testimony period, the propounding party may file a notice of reliance, pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(j)(3)(i), on the request for admission, the exhibits thereto, and its adversary's response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative methods include (a) taking a discovery deposition, marking documents as exhibits and having the witness identify them, then submitting the deposition and exhibits under a notice of reliance; or (b) combining a request for production with a notice to take the adversary's deposition (asking the deponent to bring the documents). See accompanying case examples (ProQuest, Kohler) and TBMP Chapter 700 for full discussion of making evidence of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for combined request for production and deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A party served with a request for production has thirty days from service to respond, plus an extra five days if service was by first-class mail, Express Mail, or overnight courier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a discovery deposition must be both noticed and taken before the end of the discovery period, a combined notice/request for production normally must be served at least thirty-five days prior to the close of discovery. See TBMP § 403.03 and § 403.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions must be noticed and taken before discovery closes
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be both noticed and taken prior to the expiration of the discovery period (unless the parties stipulate that the deposition may be taken outside of the period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a strict timing requirement (see Fed. R. Civ. P. 30 and TBMP § 403.02). Case law (e.g., National Football League v. DNH Management LLC) supports that depositions must be 'taken' within discovery even if 'served' timing differs for interrogatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling courtesy and parties' duty to cooperate
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of convenience and courtesy and to avoid scheduling conflicts, the parties should attempt to schedule depositions by agreement rather than unilaterally setting a deposition date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a party may notice a deposition, it is common and encouraged to discuss alternative dates. The parties have a duty to cooperate in resolving scheduling conflicts (see TBMP § 408; Sunrider Corp. v. Raats; Luehrmann v. Kwik Kopy Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be deposed — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may, by oral questions, depose any person, including a party, without leave of court except as provided in Rule 30(a)(2); the deponent's attendance may be compelled by subpoena under Rule 45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery depositions generally may be taken of any person, whether or not the person is a party, and whether or not the person resides in the United States. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a) and TBMP § 404.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Board permission (leave) is required to take a deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave of the court (Board) is required to take a deposition if: (A) the deposition would result in more than ten depositions being taken by plaintiffs or by defendants or third-party defendants; (B) the deponent has already been deposed in the case; (C) the party seeks to take the deposition before the time specified in Rule 26(d) without certifying expected unavailability; or (D) the deponent is confined in prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2) and Board practice—Board permission must be obtained under these circumstances. See TBMP § 404.02 and accompanying notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of deposition within the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposition of a natural person shall be taken in the Federal judicial district where the person resides or is regularly employed or at any place on which the parties agree by stipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deposition may be taken either orally or on written questions in the manner described in 37 CFR § 2.124. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 30 and 31; TBMP § 404.03(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Party deponent in U.S.: notice alone; nonparty: responsibility to secure attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed deponent residing in the United States is a party (or an officer, director, managing agent of a party, or a Rule 30(b)(6)/31(a)(4) designee), the deposition may be taken on notice alone. If the proposed deponent is not a party, the deposing party bears the responsibility to secure attendance; if voluntary appearance is not obtained, attendance must be secured by subpoena under 35 U.S.C. § 24 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a noticed party deponent fails to appear, the deposing party may seek to compel attendance by motion to compel (see TBMP § 523). For nonparty witnesses, subpoenas must be issued from the U.S. district court in the district where the deponent resides or is regularly employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena issuance and enforcement limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The subpoena to compel attendance at a discovery deposition must be issued from the United States district court in the federal judicial district where the deponent resides or is regularly employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person named in a subpoena fails to attend or refuses to answer, enforcement must be sought from the U.S. District Court that issued the subpoena; the Board has no jurisdiction to enforce or quash subpoenas. See Dan Foam ApS v. Sleep Innovations Inc., Luehrmann v. Kwik Kopy, and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign person depositions — party present in foreign country
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery deposition of a natural person residing in a foreign country who is a party (or officer, director, managing agent, or Rule 30(b)(6)/31 designee) shall, if taken in a foreign country, be taken in the manner prescribed by § 2.124 unless the Board, upon motion for good cause, orders or the parties stipulate that the deposition be taken by oral examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a deposition may be taken on notice alone. Parties contemplating foreign depositions should consult local counsel and Office of Citizens Consular Services to determine whether the foreign country permits such depositions and what procedures apply. See TBMP § 404.03(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign person depositions — considerations and sanctions factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Some foreign laws may preclude taking depositions for use in U.S. proceedings; in determining sanctions for non-compliance due to conflict with foreign laws, factors considered include (1) the good faith of the non-complying party; (2) whether the non-complying party would incur foreign criminal liability; and (3) whether alternative sources of information are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should investigate foreign law and policy and consult the Department of State before seeking foreign depositions. See TBMP § 404.03(b) notes and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign nonparty willing to appear
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonparty natural person who resides in a foreign country but is willing to appear voluntarily may be deposed in the same manner as a foreign party (i.e., per TBMP § 404.03(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even willing witnesses may be subject to foreign prohibitions or procedures; consult local counsel or Department of State resources before proceeding. See TBMP § 404.03(c)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign nonparty unwilling — letter rogatory / Hague Convention procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no certain procedure, but a party may seek the discovery deposition of an unwilling foreign nonparty through (a) a letter rogatory (letter of request) transmitted via the Department of State, or (b) the Hague Convention letter-of-request procedure where applicable; each has procedural requirements and uncertainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter rogatory requirements: file a written request with the Board; submit an original and two copies of the proposed letter and questions (and translations if needed); serve copies on adverse parties; allow cross and redirect questions; Board signs and authenticates the letter and forwards to the Department of State; the propounding party must pay all consular/foreign fees and may be required to make a deposit. The process can take months or years, may suspend Board proceedings, may not be executed by the foreign authority, and executed depositions may have limited probative value because foreign procedures differ. The Hague Convention is an alternative in Convention countries but Board cautions that letter rogatory may be more likely honored. See TBMP § 404.03(c)(2) and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign person present within the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a foreign party or a person who consents to testify on its behalf is or will be present within the United States during discovery, such person may be deposed by oral examination upon notice (37 CFR § 2.120(c)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deposition must be taken in the federal judicial district where the witness resides or is regularly employed, or where the witness is at the time of deposition. This option supplements other procedures for foreign depositions. See TBMP § 404.03(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons before whom depositions may be taken
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the United States, a deposition must be taken before (A) an officer authorized to administer oaths by federal law or the law of the place of examination, or (B) a person appointed by the court where the action is pending to administer oaths and take testimony. In a foreign country, depositions may be taken under treaty, letter of request, on notice before a person authorized to administer oaths by federal or local law, or before a person commissioned by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fed. R. Civ. P. 28 governs these issues. A deposition must not be taken before a person who is any party's relative, employee, or attorney; related to or employed by any party's attorney; or financially interested in the action. Board depositions follow the persons designated by Fed. R. Civ. P. 28. See TBMP § 404.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness fees and travel expenses for subpoenaed witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Every witness subpoenaed and in attendance shall be allowed the fees and traveling expenses allowed to witnesses attending the United States district courts (35 U.S.C. § 24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A witness served with a subpoena cannot be held in contempt for disobeying unless his fees and traveling expenses in going to and returning from, and one day's attendance at, the place of examination are paid or tendered at the time of service; refusals to disclose secret matters may also require court orders. See 35 U.S.C. § 24 and accompanying notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence taken under a letter of request need not be excluded for procedural departures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence obtained in response to a letter of request need not be excluded merely because it is not a verbatim transcript, because the testimony was not taken under oath, or because of similar departures from U.S. deposition requirements (Fed. R. Civ. P. 28(b)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When foreign procedures differ, the Board will consider those differences when determining the probative value of the deposition rather than automatically excluding the evidence. See TBMP § 404.04 and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposition on written questions option and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions (including testimony depositions) may be taken on written questions in the manner described in 37 CFR § 2.124 (for discovery) and 37 CFR § 2.123(a)(2) (for testimony), subject to Board rules and motions for oral examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 404.07 for full procedure on depositions on written questions. Parties should review 37 CFR §§ 2.120–2.124 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 30, 31, and 28 for procedural detail.
